claim: Modulation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling in mouse thymic epithelial cells (TECs) disrupts embryonic thymus organogenesis.
source: Previous findings showed that modulation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling in mouse thymic epithelial cells (TECs) disrupts embryonic thymus organogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research findings.

claim: Gain-of-function (GOF) of β-catenin in TECs results in severe thymic dysplasia and T-cell deficiency beginning from the embryonic period.
source: We found that GOF of β-catenin in TECs results in severe thymic dysplasia and T-cell deficiency beginning from the embryonic period.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing thymic dysplasia and T-cell deficiency in β-cat GOF mice.

claim: Loss-of-function (LOF) of β-catenin in TECs reduces the number of cortical TECs and thymocytes modestly and only postnatally.
source: By contrast, LOF of β-catenin in TECs reduces the number of cortical TECs and thymocytes modestly and only postnatally.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced cTEC and thymocyte numbers in postnatal β-cat LOF mice.

claim: Fine-tuning of β-catenin expression within a permissive range is required for TECs to generate an optimal microenvironment to support postnatal T-cell development.
source: These results indicate that fine-tuning of β-catenin expression within a permissive range is required for TECs to generate an optimal microenvironment to support postnatal T-cell development.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined GOF and LOF experimental results.

claim: The thymus is an organ where lymphocyte progenitors differentiate into functionally competent T cells through interactions primarily with cortical thymic epithelial cells (cTECs) and medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTECs).
source: The thymus is an organ where lymphocyte progenitors differentiate into functionally competent T cells through interactions primarily with cortical thymic epithelial cells (cTECs) and medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTECs), which construct a three-dimensional epithelial network of the thymus and facilitate the development and selection of developing T cells.
evidence: This claim represents established scientific knowledge about thymus function.

claim: Thymus organogenesis is initiated around embryonic day 11 (E11) in mouse.
source: To establish a functional thymic microenvironment, the thymus organogenesis is tightly regulated by the interaction of thymic epithelial cells (TECs) with neighboring cells, such as mesenchymal cells and hematopoietic cells, through various molecules including morphogens, growth factors, cytokines, and chemokines, during the thymus organogenesis that is initiated around embryonic day 11 (E11) in mouse (Blackburn and Manley, 2004; Gordon and Manley, 2011; Takahama et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway has been implicated in thymus development following the discovery of its core components, T-cell factor (TCF)/lymphoid enhancing factor (LEF) family transcription factors, in developing thymocytes.
source: The Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway has been implicated in thymus development following the discovery of its core components, T-cell factor (TCF)/lymphoid enhancing factor (LEF) family transcription factors, in developing thymocytes (Oosterwegel et al., 1991; Travis et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Wnt proteins activate the canonical signaling pathway through interaction with their receptors of the Frizzled family and coreceptors of the LRP5/6 family.
source: Wnt proteins activate the canonical signaling pathway through interaction with their receptors of the Frizzled family and coreceptors of the LRP5/6 family.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about Wnt signaling mechanisms.

claim: The systemic deletion of Wnt4 reduces the number of TECs as well as thymocytes.
source: The systemic deletion of Wnt4, which is abundant in embryonic TECs (Pongracz et al., 2003), reduces the number of TECs as well as thymocytes (Heinonen et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Keratin 5 (Krt5) promoter-driven inhibition of Wnt/β-catenin signaling by the overexpression of Wnt inhibitor Dickkopf1 (DKK1) or by the deficiency of β-catenin reduces the number of TECs including K5+K8+ immature TECs.
source: Keratin 5 (Krt5) promoter-driven inhibition of Wnt/β-catenin signaling by the overexpression of Wnt inhibitor Dickkopf1 (DKK1) or by the deficiency of β-catenin reduces the number of TECs including K5+K8+ immature TECs (Osada et al., 2010; Liang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A reduction in the number of TECs is observed in perinatal mice in which β-catenin is deleted using Foxn1-Cre.
source: Similarly, a reduction in the number of TECs is observed in perinatal mice in which β-catenin is deleted using Foxn1-Cre, which targets TECs expressing transcription factor Forkhead box N1 (Foxn1) (Swann et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Foxn1-Cre-mediated β-catenin deletion causes neonatal lethality due to side effects in the skin epidermis.
source: However, the Foxn1-Cre-mediated β-catenin deletion causes neonatal lethality due to side effects in the skin epidermis, so that the postnatal effects of β-catenin deficiency in TECs remain unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Overactivation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling by the deletion of transmembrane protein Kremen 1 results in the increase in the number of K5+K8+ immature TECs and the disorganization of the TEC network.
source: On the other hand, overactivation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling by the deletion of transmembrane protein Kremen 1, which binds to DKK1 and potentiates Wnt signaling inhibition, results in the increase in the number of K5+K8+ immature TECs and the disorganization of the TEC network by the decrease in the frequency of mature cTECs and mTECs (Osada et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Keratin 14 (Krt14) promoter-driven loss of APC disorganizes the thymus and reduces its size.
source: Keratin 14 (Krt14) promoter-driven loss of APC disorganizes the thymus and reduces its size (Kuraguchi et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The overexpression of β-catenin using Foxn1-Cre causes a more severe defect in embryonic thymus development, which is accompanied by the failure of separation of the thymic primordium from the parathyroid primordium.
source: The overexpression of β-catenin using Foxn1-Cre causes a more severe defect in embryonic thymus development, which is accompanied by the failure of separation of the thymic primordium from the parathyroid primordium (Zuklys et al., 2009; Swann et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Thymus-specific proteasome subunit β5t is specifically expressed in cTECs in a Foxn1-dependent manner.
source: Thymus-specific proteasome subunit β5t is specifically expressed in cTECs in a Foxn1-dependent manner, and is important for the generation of functionally competent CD8+ T cells (Murata et al., 2007; Ohigashi et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: β5t in postnatal mice is exclusively expressed by cTECs but not mTECs.
source: β5t in postnatal mice is exclusively expressed by cTECs but not mTECs (Ripen et al., 2011; Uddin et al., 2017); however, its transcription is also detectable in embryonic TECs that differentiate into cTECs and mTECs (Ohigashi et al., 2013; Ohigashi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: β5t transcription is detectable in embryonic TECs that differentiate into cTECs and mTECs.
source: β5t in postnatal mice is exclusively expressed by cTECs but not mTECs (Ripen et al., 2011; Uddin et al., 2017); however, its transcription is also detectable in embryonic TECs that differentiate into cTECs and mTECs (Ohigashi et al., 2013; Ohigashi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: β5t-Cre enables highly efficient and specific genetic manipulation in TECs without side effects in the skin epidermis.
source: By taking advantage of the highly specific Cre activity only in TECs and not in skin epidermal cells in β5t-iCre mice, here we engineered gain-of-function (GOF) and loss-of-function (LOF) of β-catenin specifically in TECs and addressed the contribution of the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway in TECs, focusing on the effects of thymus function on T-cell development during the postnatal period.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data demonstrating the specificity of β5t-iCre.

claim: β5t-Cre-mediated GOF of β-catenin showed no disruption of the thoracic migration of the embryonic thymus.
source: Contrary to previous studies demonstrating that the Foxn1-Cre-mediated GOF of β-catenin perturbed the migration of the thymic primordium from the pharyngeal region into the thoracic cavity during the embryogenesis (Zuklys et al., 2009; Swann et al., 2017), the β5t-Cre-mediated GOF of β-catenin (β-cat GOF) showed no disruption of the thoracic migration of the embryonic thymus (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: The thymus in β-cat GOF mice showed severe dysplasia by E15.5.
source: However, the thymus in these mice showed severe dysplasia by E15.5 (Figure 1B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: β-cat GOF embryos appeared normal in size and exhibited undisturbed limb development.
source: The β-cat GOF embryos appeared normal in size (Figure 1B) and exhibited undisturbed limb development (data not shown), indicating that the thymic dysplasia in β-cat GOF mice occurred independent of systemic retardation in embryogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: β5t-Cre-mediated tdTomato-expressing cells were specifically detected in the thymus in the thoracic cavity in both control and β-cat GOF mice at E15.5.
source: Fluorescence detection of Cre-mediated recombination by further crossing to R26R-tdTomato reporter mice (Madisen et al., 2010) revealed that β5t-Cre-mediated tdTomato-expressing cells were specifically detected in the thymus in the thoracic cavity in both control and β-cat GOF mice at E15.5, further confirming that TECs successfully migrated into the thoracic cavity in β-cat GOF mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B using tdTomato reporter mice.

claim: In control mice, tdTomato-labeled cells distributed uniformly throughout the thymus, whereas in β-cat GOF mice, tdTomato-labeled cells densely distributed in concentric mid-inner layers, excluding the central core.
source: Unlike control mice in which tdTomato-labeled cells distributed uniformly throughout the thymus, tdTomato-labeled cells in β-cat GOF mice densely distributed in concentric mid-inner layers, excluding the central core, in the thymus (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A multilayered concentric structure of epithelial cells surrounding the central core was observed in E15.5 β-cat GOF embryos.
source: Morphological alteration of the thymus was apparent in sagittal sections of E15.5 β-cat GOF embryos by hematoxylin and eosin staining and by the detection of keratin 5 (K5) and keratin 8 (K8) expression, in which a multilayered concentric structure of epithelial cells surrounding the central core that mainly consisted of nonepithelial structures sparsely containing erythrocytes was observed (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: β-Catenin was abundant in the concentric layers of the thymus in E15.5 β-cat GOF mice.
source: β-Catenin was abundant in the concentric layers of the thymus in E15.5 β-cat GOF mice, whereas β5t was undetectable throughout the E15.5 β-cat GOF thymus (Figure 1C), indicating that GOF of β-catenin in TECs diminishes β5t expression in TECs.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: β5t was undetectable throughout the E15.5 β-cat GOF thymus.
source: β-Catenin was abundant in the concentric layers of the thymus in E15.5 β-cat GOF mice, whereas β5t was undetectable throughout the E15.5 β-cat GOF thymus (Figure 1C), indicating that GOF of β-catenin in TECs diminishes β5t expression in TECs.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: GOF of β-catenin in TECs diminishes β5t expression in TECs.
source: β-Catenin was abundant in the concentric layers of the thymus in E15.5 β-cat GOF mice, whereas β5t was undetectable throughout the E15.5 β-cat GOF thymus (Figure 1C), indicating that GOF of β-catenin in TECs diminishes β5t expression in TECs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that β5t is undetectable in β-cat GOF thymus.

claim: The intracellular level of β-catenin in TECs from β-cat GOF mice was increased by 70% compared with that from control mice at E15.5.
source: Intracellular staining of β-catenin in CD45−EpCAM+ TECs isolated from E15.5 thymus revealed that the intracellular level of β-catenin in TECs from β-cat GOF mice was increased by 70% compared with that from control mice (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The expression of Foxn1 was detected in the thymic primordium in both β-cat GOF and control embryos at E11.5.
source: The expression of Foxn1, a transcription factor that characterizes the thymic epithelium-specified domain of the third pharyngeal pouch (Nehls et al., 1994; Gordon et al., 2001), was detected in the thymic primordium in both β-cat GOF and control embryos at E11.5, indicating that the initiation of the earliest thymus organogenesis is undisturbed in β-cat GOF mice (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The initiation of the earliest thymus organogenesis is undisturbed in β-cat GOF mice.
source: The expression of Foxn1, a transcription factor that characterizes the thymic epithelium-specified domain of the third pharyngeal pouch (Nehls et al., 1994; Gordon et al., 2001), was detected in the thymic primordium in both β-cat GOF and control embryos at E11.5, indicating that the initiation of the earliest thymus organogenesis is undisturbed in β-cat GOF mice (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Foxn1 expression is detected in β-cat GOF embryos at E11.5.

claim: The colonization of CD45+ lymphocytes in Foxn1-expressing thymic primordium was observed in both β-cat GOF and control embryos at E12.5.
source: At E12.5, when the expression of β5t becomes detectable in the thymus (Ripen et al., 2011), the colonization of CD45+ lymphocytes in Foxn1-expressing thymic primordium was observed in both β-cat GOF and control embryos (Figure 2A), further supporting that early thymus organogenesis is undisturbed in β-cat GOF mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The thymus morphology was markedly altered in β-cat GOF embryos at E13.5.
source: However, the thymus morphology was markedly altered in β-cat GOF embryos at E13.5, namely, the thymic primordium appeared spherical in β-cat GOF embryos and ovoid in control embryos (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: At E13.5 in β-cat GOF embryos, Foxn1+ TECs and CD45+ lymphocytes accumulated preferentially in the anterior area of the thymic primordium.
source: At this stage in β-cat GOF embryos, Foxn1+ TECs and CD45+ lymphocytes accumulated preferentially in the anterior area of the thymic primordium (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: By E15.5, Foxn1 expression became undetectable and the number of CD45+ lymphocytes was markedly reduced in the dysplastic thymus in β-cat GOF embryos.
source: By E15.5, Foxn1 expression became undetectable and the number of CD45+ lymphocytes was markedly reduced in the dysplastic thymus in β-cat GOF embryos (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The expression of Wnt/β-catenin target genes, including Axin2, Dkk1, and Msx1, was upregulated in β-cat GOF TECs at E15.5.
source: Quantitative RT-PCR analysis of CD45−EpCAM+ TECs isolated from E15.5 thymus established that the expression of Wnt/β-catenin target genes, including Axin2, Dkk1, and Msx1, was upregulated in β-cat GOF TECs (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The expression of Foxn1, Psmb11, and Ccl25 was significantly reduced in β-cat GOF TECs at E15.5.
source: By contrast, the expression of genes functionally relevant to TECs, such as Foxn1, Psmb11 (encoding β5t protein), and Ccl25 (encoding chemokine CCL25 protein that attracts lymphocyte progenitors to the thymic primordium; Liu et al., 2006), was significantly reduced in β-cat GOF TECs, consistent with the results of immunohistochemical analysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The expression of Dll4 was markedly reduced in β-cat GOF TECs at E15.5.
source: The expression of Delta-like (Dll) 4, a Foxn1-dependent Notch ligand essential for early T-cell development (Hozumi et al., 2008; Koch et al., 2008), was markedly reduced in β-cat GOF TECs (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The expression of involucrin (Ivl), loricrin (Lor), and desmoglein-1 alpha (Dsg1a) genes was upregulated in β-cat GOF TECs but not control TECs at E15.5.
source: Notably, the expression of involucrin (Ivl), loricrin (Lor), and desmoglein-1 alpha (Dsg1a) genes by the terminally differentiated keratinocytes (Candi et al., 2005) and the terminally differentiated subpopulation of mTECs (Yano et al., 2008; Michel et al., 2017) was upregulated in β-cat GOF TECs but not control TECs at E15.5 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Normal differentiation of TECs is disrupted in β-cat GOF embryos.
source: These results suggest that normal differentiation of TECs is disrupted in β-cat GOF embryos; instead, embryonic TECs exhibit aberrant differentiation into epithelial cells that partially share gene expression profiles with the terminally differentiated keratinocytes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the gene expression data showing upregulation of keratinocyte markers.

claim: Embryonic TECs in β-cat GOF mice exhibit aberrant differentiation into epithelial cells that partially share gene expression profiles with the terminally differentiated keratinocytes.
source: These results suggest that normal differentiation of TECs is disrupted in β-cat GOF embryos; instead, embryonic TECs exhibit aberrant differentiation into epithelial cells that partially share gene expression profiles with the terminally differentiated keratinocytes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the gene expression data showing upregulation of keratinocyte markers.

claim: The number of CD45+ thymocytes in E15.5 thymus was significantly reduced in β-cat GOF mice compared with control mice.
source: The number of CD45+ thymocytes in E15.5 thymus was significantly reduced in β-cat GOF mice compared with control mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The majority of E15.5 thymocytes in β-cat GOF mice and control mice were equivalently CD4−CD8− double negative (DN).
source: Flow cytometric analysis of CD45+ thymocytes indicated that the majority of E15.5 thymocytes in β-cat GOF mice and control mice were equivalently CD4−CD8− double negative (DN) (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data.

claim: The DN thymocytes in β-cat GOF embryos were predominantly arrested at CD44+CD25− DN1 stage.
source: However, the DN thymocytes in β-cat GOF embryos were predominantly arrested at CD44+CD25− DN1 stage (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The numbers of downstream thymocytes at DN2, DN3, and DN4 stages were dramatically reduced in β-cat GOF embryos compared with control embryos.
source: Indeed, the numbers of downstream thymocytes at DN2 (CD44+CD25+), DN3 (CD44−CD25+), and DN4 (CD44−CD25−) stages were dramatically reduced in β-cat GOF embryos compared with control embryos, whereas the number of DN1 thymocytes was comparable between β-cat GOF and control embryos (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The number of DN1 thymocytes was comparable between β-cat GOF and control embryos at E15.5.
source: Indeed, the numbers of downstream thymocytes at DN2 (CD44+CD25+), DN3 (CD44−CD25+), and DN4 (CD44−CD25−) stages were dramatically reduced in β-cat GOF embryos compared with control embryos, whereas the number of DN1 thymocytes was comparable between β-cat GOF and control embryos (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: β-Cat GOF mice grew to adulthood with no gross abnormality in appearance and body weight.
source: β-Cat GOF mice grew to adulthood with no gross abnormality in appearance and body weight (Figure 3A, B), whereas the thymic dysplasia persisted throughout the postnatal periods in β-cat GOF mice (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by observational data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: The thymic dysplasia persisted throughout the postnatal periods in β-cat GOF mice.
source: β-Cat GOF mice grew to adulthood with no gross abnormality in appearance and body weight (Figure 3A, B), whereas the thymic dysplasia persisted throughout the postnatal periods in β-cat GOF mice (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by observational data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The frequency and the number of αβTCR-expressing T cells in the spleen and the inguinal lymph node (iLN) were significantly reduced in β-cat GOF adult mice.
source: Flow cytometric analysis of cells from postnatal lymphoid organs showed that the frequency and the number of αβTCR-expressing T cells in the spleen and the inguinal lymph node (iLN) were significantly reduced in β-cat GOF adult mice (Figure 4A, B), indicating that αβ T cells are essentially lost in β-cat GOF mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: αβ T cells are essentially lost in β-cat GOF mice.
source: Flow cytometric analysis of cells from postnatal lymphoid organs showed that the frequency and the number of αβTCR-expressing T cells in the spleen and the inguinal lymph node (iLN) were significantly reduced in β-cat GOF adult mice (Figure 4A, B), indicating that αβ T cells are essentially lost in β-cat GOF mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the significant reduction in αβTCR-expressing T cells.

claim: The reduction of γδ TCR-expressing T cells was detected in β-cat GOF mice.
source: We also detected the reduction of γδ TCR-expressing T cells in β-cat GOF mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data.

claim: Vγ5+ γδT cells were severely reduced in frequency in the embryonic thymus and the postnatal skin of β-cat GOF mice.
source: Vγ5+ γδT cells, which are generated in the embryonic thymus and localize to the epidermis to form dendritic epidermal T cells (DETCs) in adult mice (Havran and Allison, 1988), were severely reduced in frequency in the embryonic thymus and the postnatal skin of β-cat GOF mice (Figure 4C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: Vγ4+ and Vγ1+ γδT cells were reduced in frequency in the iLN and the spleen of β-cat GOF adult mice.
source: Vγ4+ and Vγ1+ γδT cells, which are generated in the thymus during the perinatal period subsequently to the embryonic generation of Vγ5+ γδT cells (Pereira et al., 1995), were similarly reduced in frequency in the iLN and the spleen of β-cat GOF adult mice (Figure 4E, data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The thymus-dependent γδT cells, including Vγ5+, Vγ4+, and Vγ1+ γδT cells, are essentially lost in β-cat GOF mice.
source: These results indicate that the thymus-dependent γδT cells, including Vγ5+, Vγ4+, and Vγ1+ γδT cells, are essentially lost in β-cat GOF mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the reduction in various γδT cell populations.

claim: Morphological abnormality in the thymus was not apparent in β-cat LOF embryos at E15.5.
source: In contrast to β-cat GOF mice, morphological abnormality in the thymus was not apparent in β-cat LOF embryos at E15.5 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by observational data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Immunohistofluorescence analysis confirmed the reduction of β-catenin in the thymus of β-cat LOF mice at E15.5.
source: Immunohistofluorescence analysis confirmed the reduction of β-catenin in the thymus of β-cat LOF mice at E15.5, whereas the expression of Foxn1, K5, and K8 in E15.5 thymus was comparable between β-cat LOF mice and littermate control mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The expression of Foxn1, K5, and K8 in E15.5 thymus was comparable between β-cat LOF mice and littermate control mice.
source: Immunohistofluorescence analysis confirmed the reduction of β-catenin in the thymus of β-cat LOF mice at E15.5, whereas the expression of Foxn1, K5, and K8 in E15.5 thymus was comparable between β-cat LOF mice and littermate control mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Intracellular β-catenin level was reduced by 77% in CD45−EpCAM+ TECs of β-cat LOF mice at E15.5.
source: Flow cytometric analysis revealed that intracellular β-catenin level was reduced by 77% in CD45−EpCAM+ TECs of β-cat LOF mice at E15.5 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The number of total thymic cells and the frequency and the number of total TECs and UEA1−Ly51+ cTECs were comparable between β-cat LOF and control mice at E15.5.
source: However, the number of total thymic cells and the frequency and the number of total TECs and UEA1−Ly51+ cTECs were comparable between β-cat LOF and control mice (Figure 5D, E), indicating that β5t-Cre-mediated loss of β-catenin in TECs did not alter embryonic thymus development by E15.5.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5D and 5E.

claim: β5t-Cre-mediated loss of β-catenin in TECs did not alter embryonic thymus development by E15.5.
source: However, the number of total thymic cells and the frequency and the number of total TECs and UEA1−Ly51+ cTECs were comparable between β-cat LOF and control mice (Figure 5D, E), indicating that β5t-Cre-mediated loss of β-catenin in TECs did not alter embryonic thymus development by E15.5.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparable TEC numbers between β-cat LOF and control mice.

claim: β-Cat LOF mice grew to adulthood with normal hair coat.
source: β-Cat LOF mice grew to adulthood with normal hair coat (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by observational data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Thymus size in β-cat LOF mice was noticeably reduced in comparison to that in control mice during the postnatal period.
source: However, thymus size in β-cat LOF mice was noticeably reduced in comparison to that in control mice during the postnatal period (Figure 6B), with concomitant reductions in thymus weight but not body weight (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by observational data shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: Thymus weight was reduced in β-cat LOF mice during the postnatal period.
source: However, thymus size in β-cat LOF mice was noticeably reduced in comparison to that in control mice during the postnatal period (Figure 6B), with concomitant reductions in thymus weight but not body weight (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurement data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Body weight was not reduced in β-cat LOF mice during the postnatal period.
source: However, thymus size in β-cat LOF mice was noticeably reduced in comparison to that in control mice during the postnatal period (Figure 6B), with concomitant reductions in thymus weight but not body weight (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurement data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The β-catenin expression was effectively reduced by 96% in UEA1−Ly51+ cTECs and by 94% in UEA1+Ly51− mTECs in β-cat LOF mice at 2 wk old.
source: Flow cytometric analysis revealed that the β-catenin expression was effectively reduced by 96% in UEA1−Ly51+ cTECs and by 94% in UEA1+Ly51− mTECs in β-cat LOF mice at 2 wk old (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Quantitative RT-PCR analysis showed marked reduction of β-catenin mRNA (Ctnnb1) expression in cTECs and mTECs of β-cat LOF mice.
source: Accordingly, quantitative RT-PCR analysis showed marked reduction of β-catenin mRNA (Ctnnb1) expression in cTECs and mTECs of β-cat LOF mice (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The frequency and the number of cTECs were decreased in the thymus of β-cat LOF mice at 2 wk compared with control mice.
source: In the thymus of β-cat LOF mice, the frequency and the number of cTECs were decreased compared with control mice (Figure 7C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7C and 7D.

claim: Axin2 expression in cTECs was significantly reduced in β-cat LOF mice at 2 wk.
source: Axin2 expression in cTECs was significantly reduced in β-cat LOF mice, indicating that Wnt/β-catenin signals were efficiently impaired in cTECs from β-cat LOF mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin signals were efficiently impaired in cTECs from β-cat LOF mice.
source: Axin2 expression in cTECs was significantly reduced in β-cat LOF mice, indicating that Wnt/β-catenin signals were efficiently impaired in cTECs from β-cat LOF mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the reduction in Axin2 expression, a Wnt/β-catenin target gene.

claim: The expression of Foxn1, Il7, and Cxcl12 was not altered in cTECs from β-cat LOF mice at 2 wk.
source: However, the expression of Foxn1, Il7, and Cxcl12, which encode functionally important molecules in cTECs, was not altered in cTECs from β-cat LOF mice (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The cellularity of mTECs was not altered in β-cat LOF mice at 2 wk.
source: On the other hand, despite that the expression of β-catenin in mTECs was markedly reduced in β-cat LOF mice, the cellularity of mTECs was not altered in β-cat LOF mice (Figure 7C, D), and the expression of Axin2 was not reduced in mTECs from β-cat LOF mice (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7C and 7D.
